tool.name: ShadowPolygons

summary.para:
View online help files: https://www.jennessent.com/cartography/create-shadow-polygons.html
Creates concentric ring buffers around the (dissolved) polygons of a feature class, with a Transparency attribute that fades outward, so the rings render as a soft black cartographic shadow that makes the source features stand out. The shadow has the controls of the Graphic Background tools' drop shadow: a size and spread for its soft edge, and a distance and light angle to shift it.

tool.usage:
The tool dissolves the input feature class into a single source polygon and builds a series of ring buffers around it. If the input layer has selected polygons, only those are dissolved and used; otherwise every polygon in the feature class is dissolved into the source.
Each ring is stored as its own polygon with a Transparency value that increases from the innermost ring outward. When the rings are drawn in solid black with the fill transparency varying by the Transparency field, the innermost ring is the most opaque and each successive ring is more transparent, creating a shadow that fades away from the source features. The output carries a Buffer_Size field (the ring's outer distance, in meters; 0 for the source polygon) and a Transparency field (percent); when the output is a shapefile, whose field names are limited to 10 characters, they are named BufferSize and Transp_Pct, and the layer file is bound to Transp_Pct. The dissolved source polygon is included in the output with a Transparency of 100 (fully transparent), so it never obscures the real features drawn on top of it. A layer file symbolized this way is created next to the output feature class (in the folder that holds a geodatabase output). An output written to the memory workspace has no folder, so its layer file goes to the ArcGIS Pro scratch folder; the layer on the map is symbolized all the same. An in-memory feature class is temporary by nature, and so is that layer file.
You choose the number of rings and the size of the soft edge. The size, and the shadow distance below, can be given as a proportion of the width or the height of the source polygon's extent, or as an absolute distance in meters, kilometers, feet, or miles. The soft edge is cut into that many equal rings, and the transparency falls from nearly 100 percent at the outer edge to the minimum transparency at the inner edge along a smooth S-curve, the profile the Graphic Background tools' drop shadow uses.
The shadow can be shifted and its edge spread, as a drop shadow in a graphics program can. The illumination source is the compass direction the light comes from, 0 to 360 degrees clockwise from north (0 is light from the north, 315 from the northwest), and the shadow distance is how far the shadow is shifted away from the light; 0 leaves it centered on the source, a glow. The spread is how much of the soft edge is made solid: 0 centers the soft edge on the shadow's outline (half of it inside), 50 puts the whole soft edge outside the outline (the tool's original behavior and its default), and 100 gives a hard-edged shadow grown by the size. Every piece of the shadow has the source polygon cut out of it, since the shadow lies beneath the source.
If the source feature class uses a geographic coordinate system, the rings are buffered geodesically so they are correctly shaped on the ground. The tool honors the Output Coordinate System environment (the finished output is projected into it).
Because the rings are purely for cartographic effect, the source polygon is generalized slightly before buffering, so the rings are approximate and lightweight rather than an exact analytical buffer.

dialogReference.para: The polygon feature class or layer to build the shadow around. If the layer has a selection, only the selected polygons are dissolved into the source; otherwise all polygons are dissolved together.

The output polygon feature class of ring buffers. It contains one record per ring plus the dissolved source polygon, with Buffer_Size and Transparency fields. A matching layer file is written beside it.
How many ring buffers to create around the source polygon. The default is 10. Each ring is one step of the outermost size, spaced evenly from the source outward.

param.name: size_value
param.displayname: Size of the soft edge (outermost buffer)

dialogReference.para: The width of the shadow's soft edge: with the default spread of 50, the distance from the source polygon to the outer edge of the outermost ring. Interpreted using the Units setting; when the units are a proportion of the extent, this is a fraction (for example, 0.25 means one quarter of the extent width or height).

param.name: size_units
param.displayname: Units for the size and the distance

dialogReference.para: How to interpret the size of the soft edge and the shadow distance. Choose a proportion of the source extent's width or height, or an absolute distance in meters, kilometers, feet, or miles.

The transparency, in percent, of the innermost ring (the darkest part of the shadow). The default is 50. Each successive ring outward is more transparent, up to nearly 100 percent at the outermost ring. Must be at least 0 and less than 100.

param.name: distance_value
param.displayname: Shadow distance (shift away from the light)

dialogReference.para: How far the whole shadow is shifted away from the light, in the Units chosen above. The default, 0, leaves the shadow centered on the source polygon, a glow on every side. A shifted shadow shows on the side away from the light, as a drop shadow does.

The compass direction the light comes from, 0 to 360 degrees clockwise from north: 0 is light from the north, 90 from the east, 315 (the default) from the northwest, the usual choice on a map. The shadow falls on the opposite side. It only matters when the shadow distance is more than 0.

param.name: spread
param.displayname: Spread (percent of the soft edge made solid)

dialogReference.para: How much of the soft edge is made solid, from 0 to 100 percent. 0 centers the soft edge on the shadow's outline, half inside and half outside, the softest edge. 50 (the default) puts the whole soft edge outside the outline, which is what this tool has always done. 100 makes a hard-edged shadow grown by the size. Whatever the spread, the source polygon itself is cut out of every piece.

scriptExample.title: Create Shadow Polygons example (stand-alone script)
scriptExample.para: Build a 10-ring drop shadow: a soft edge one tenth of the source extent width, shifted a twentieth of the width away from a light in the northwest, with the innermost ring at 40 percent transparency.
scriptExample.code: import arcpy arcpy.ImportToolbox(r"C:\path\to\JennessEnterprisesTools.pyt") # your installed path is shown in this tool's run messages arcpy.jenness.ShadowPolygons( in_features=r"C:\Project\Study.gdb\StudyArea", out_fc=r"C:\Project\Study.gdb\StudyArea_Shadow", num_rings=10, size_value=0.1, size_units="Proportion of extent width", min_transparency=40, distance_value=0.05, angle=315, spread=0)

dataIdInfo.idPurp: Creates fading concentric ring buffers around a polygon as a soft cartographic shadow.
dataIdInfo.idAbs: Creates concentric ring buffers around the dissolved polygons of a feature class, with a Transparency attribute that increases outward. Drawn in black with transparency varied by that field, the rings form a soft shadow that makes the source features stand out. The shadow can be shifted away from a light direction and its soft edge spread, with the controls of the Graphic Background tools' drop shadow. Selected polygons are used if the input layer has a selection, otherwise all polygons; geographic inputs are buffered geodesically. The dissolved source polygon is included with Transparency 100. The rings are approximate (the source is generalized first) and intended for cartographic effect, not analysis.
